I Drove It to My Garage in 1999 and Abandoned It: 1972 Pontiac Is a Forgotten Restoration Candidate
29 photos
Photo: eBay seller dmcal5
I drove the car to my garage in 1999, and it’s been sitting ever since. This is the description the seller of this 1972 Pontiac Firebird posted on eBay, trying to convince Internet strangers to take it home.
While this Pontiac has been sitting for so many years, it still looks doable. Sure, it’s not an easy project, and more importantly, it requires extensive work in all key areas, but with the right fixes, it would eventually become a head-turner.
The owner posted the car for auction, but a reserve has also been completed. Few specifics were shared, and I have no idea how much you need to bid to unlock the reserve. But what I do know is that the battle could soon become fiercer than expected.
Photo: eBay seller dmcal5 The 1972 Pontiac Firebird production nearly collapsed from the previous year, and it’s not because the car was no longer appealing to American buyers. Unfortunately for the Firebird, it ended up becoming a collateral victim of the UAW strike at the Norwood, Ohio plant where the Firebird and the Camaro were produced.
The strike ended after 174 days, and despite Pontiac resuming Firebird production afterwards, it ended the year with only 29,951 units rolling off the assembly line.
The base Firebird continued to be the top version in the lineup with 12,001 units, while the Esprit was the runner-up with 11,415 cars. The Formula was third in the charts with 5,249 cars, while the Trans Am was less popular than in the previous year and accounted for only 1,286 units. The Trans Am didn’t yet take off, and the strike certainly impacted its output.
The Trans Am continued to be offered with a 455 HO, once again with a manual and an automatic. The manual was the more popular choice, accounting for 458 orders.
Photo: eBay seller dmcal5 Otherwise, the Firebird could be had with a 250ci six-cylinder engine, while a 350 two-barrel was optional. This optional engine was standard on the Esprit, this time with a 400 two-barrel being listed as optional. The Formula 400 continued this year with a 400 four-barrel, while the Formula 455 was fitted from the factory with the same 455 installed on the Trans Am.
This Firebird left the factory with the Esprit package, being fitted with a 400ci V8 engine and a two-barrel carburetor. It was paired with a 400 automatic transmission.
The engine is no longer running, though it was in much better shape in 1999 when the owner drove it to their garage and parked it for eternity. The car has “not started or moved since then,” the seller explains in the post on eBay.
My recommendation is that you ask for more details about the engine under the hood because it’d be a shame to give up on the factory 400 that is still under the hood. The seller says the car is complete and original, so you should certainly give the factory 400 a second chance.
If you don’t live very far from the owner’s location, you should just send your mechanic to inspect it in person, as this is the only way to figure out all details and determine your chances of saving the engine. My guess is that an engine rebuild would do it, but you know this for sure unless you see the engine with your own eyes.
Photo: eBay seller dmcal5 The body looks good, but it wears previous accident damage. Some body parts were replaced with 1974 panels and lights, but the correct 1972 components are also included.
These aren’t the only extras that you’ll be getting if you buy this car. The Firebird also comes with two keys, the original Pontiac service manual, the owner’s manual, a title, the build sheet, and the sales brochure. This is fantastic news for someone who wants to restore the car to the day-one configuration, as all of these make this Firebird a small piece of automotive history.
There are also maintenance receipts, with the seller explaining that they appear to be complete, although they haven’t investigated this further.
It’s time to discuss the thing that could end up becoming a roadblock for this Firebird’s return to the road. The owner wants to sell the car at auction, with the bidding starting at $200, though considering a reserve is also in place, the selling price is likely much higher. No further specifics were shared, but considering the auction ends in 9 days, it’ll be interesting to see how high the bidding goes.
The vehicle is parked in Saint Louis, Missouri, and considering it no longer runs, you will need transportation to move it from its current parking location to your garage. As a result, make sure you also consider shipping costs, especially because you’ll get some extras, and a large trailer is the only option for the winning bidder.
